problem: The answer stops at p = q. That relation is true for the family, but it was obtained without using the original relation, so z has dropped out and the PDE is weaker than the proper one: the general solution of p = q is z = φ(x+y), which contains the family only as a small subfamily. It also contradicts the chapter's own rule in Section 2 (one constant → use one derivative equation plus the original relation) and the rule that the formed PDE contains z.
fix: p = ∂z/∂x = a, so a = p. Substitute into the original relation: z = p(x+y) + p². Also q = a, so equivalently p = q. Give z = p(x+y) + p² as the required PDE, and note p = q as a further relation the family satisfies.

problem: The rule is stated too loosely in two places: 'The two new equations contain a and b' is not always true (for z = a(x+y) + b the x-derivative gives only a), and 'If only one constant remains, one derivative equation plus the original relation is usually enough' leaves the reader unsure when that fails. A student may think a constant that never appears in p or q can be removed at first order.
fix: Say plainly: differentiate once in x and once in y, replace the derivatives by p and q, and combine these with the original relation. If a constant still cannot be removed this way, differentiate a second time; the PDE then becomes second order. Mention that a constant which does not appear in p or q at all cannot be removed at first order.

problem: 'A first-order PDE contains x, y, z, p and q' reads as if all five must appear. Many first-order PDEs lack one or more of them (for example q = 0, or the answer p = q in Q6, which has no z).
fix: Write: 'A first-order PDE may contain x, y, z, p and q, but contains no second derivatives such as ∂²z/∂x².'
